item.title: Hopfield Networks in Non-volatile Memory
item.description: arXiv:2610.19321v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many important computational workloads are bound by the performance of the memory system that supplies data to conventional processors. Compute in Memory (CiM) promises to circumvent this bottleneck by performing the processing within the memory. Neural Networks are memory-bound, and a notable example of such is the Hopfield Network. This work explores the design space of non-volatile computing-in-memory (NV-CiM) architectures using an instruction-level simulator to evaluate application mappings and workload-driven architectural adaptations. The exploration examines the resulting design trade-offs and includes theoretical comparisons with representative CPU and GPU architectures.
item.dc:creator: Patrick Miller, Ulya R. Karpuzcu

item.title: Cross-Layer Co-Design of Low-Latency Stateful Logic Adders with Printed Memristors
item.description: arXiv:2610.20109v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data movement between memory and processing units remains a major bottleneck in data-centric systems. Memristive Stateful Logic (SL) addresses this problem by performing Boolean operations directly on stored resistive states. However, arithmetic efficiency depends jointly on the device-supported logic primitive set, the dependency structure of the resulting operation sequence, and its mapping to datapath architectures. While prior designs typically optimize device, logic, and architecture layers separately, we jointly consider them to co-design a stateful adder. We experimentally demonstrate a mixed MAGIC and FELIX logic primitive set on printed Electrochemical Metallization (ECM) memristors and derive a full adder sequence optimized for inter-bit carry propagation. Mapping this sequence to bit-serial, bit-parallel, and bit-pipelined datapaths reduces the latter two to 2n+6 cycles for an n-bit addition. For 32-bit addition, this requires 60-88% fewer cycles than prior SL adders. Across four representative workloads, we achieve 3.7x-16.4x speedup over prior. These results show how cross-layer co-design can translate into improved workload-level performance.
item.dc:creator: Fabian Seiler, Kerem Kagan G\"ucl\"u, Hongrong Hu, Gabriel Cadilha Marques, Jasmin Aghassi-Hagmann, Nima TaheriNejad

item.title: Closed-Form Optimal Weight Splitting for Matrix-Vector Multiply on Noisy In-Memory Accelerators
item.description: arXiv:2610.20359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Analog in-memory computing performs the matrix-vector multiplications of neural networks directly inside the memory array, which saves time and energy. But each memory cell stores only a few levels and is noisy, so one cell cannot hold a weight precisely. The standard fix is to split each weight across several cells, like digits of a number. The base of this split decides the trade-off: a large base gives fine resolution but amplifies the noise, and a base near one averages the noise but wastes resolution. The best-known prior analysis considers only the noise, and so it always picks a base of one. We propose a principled method that also accounts for the limited number of levels per cell. It gives the optimal base in closed form, from a single measurement of the device noise. On a device-physics simulator, the optimal split is 3.3 dB more accurate than the common base-16 split, and it beats equal splitting in end-application accuracy.
item.dc:creator: Mehmet Aktukmak, David A. Roberts

item.title: Whose Data, Whose Benchmark? A User-Centric Framework for Auditing Evaluation Resources
item.description: arXiv:2610.19268v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Benchmarks shape how model capabilities are measured and interpreted, yet their scores can obscure whose conventions, contexts, and judgments define successful performance. We introduce a user-centric audit framework that distinguishes users who contribute benchmark content from those whose needs evaluation results are intended to represent. The framework operationalizes seven dimensions across benchmark content, metadata, documentation, and scoring procedures. Across 16 resources, we find that American-centered conventions account for 62.4-94.4% of matched signals in 11 text benchmarks, while geographic visibility in five image-text resources is concentrated and strongly associated with national GDP share (mean Pearson r = 0.780; Spearman p = 0.778). Documentation reveals a systematic source-target gap: all 16 resources operationalize source-user context, but none operationalize target-user context. Paired scoring experiments further show that meaning-preserving answer variants reduce DROP exact-match accuracy from 100.0% to 33.3%, while TruthfulQA exhibits metric-dependent reductions in reference similarity. Our framework and documentation checklist make user assumptions auditable, clarifying what benchmark scores represent and where evaluation claims are supported.
item.dc:creator: Mir Tafseer Nayeem, Davood Rafiei

item.title: Exact Cap Response and Aperture Selection for Molecular Communication under Aligned Drift
item.description: arXiv:2610.20233v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Spatial reception under directed molecule transport requires balancing useful molecule capture against intersymbol interference (ISI). To characterize this balance, we study a fully absorbing spherical receiver that counts absorption events only within a prescribed cap. Using the known joint first-hitting law under aligned drift, we derive exact cap impulse, cumulative, and eventual responses. We perform stable cumulative evaluation. We then assess the derived responses through particle simulations and time-step comparisons, and demonstrate that our conditional-timing analysis explains when opposite drifts of equal magnitude can favor the same wider aperture. We also show that for the studied geometry and a symbol duration of $0.15$ s, the aperture that maximizes the signal-to-interference difference (SID) increases from $29.13^\circ$ at zero drift to $61.86^\circ$ at a drift magnitude of $40$ $\mu$m/s. These results (i) connect joint arrival-time and location statistics to spatial reception design, (ii) characterize the tradeoff between useful molecule capture and ISI, (iii) support SID-based aperture selection for a given drift and symbol duration, and (iv) quantify the SID loss incurred by retaining the zero-drift optimal aperture for the same symbol duration.
item.dc:creator: Yen-Chi Lee, Chun-An Yang, Nan Yang

item.title: Directional and Quasi-Omnidirectional Indoor Channel Measurements at Upper 6 GHz
item.description: arXiv:2610.14890v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper presents wideband indoor channel measurements and measurement-based statistical modeling of channel parameters in the upper 6 GHz (U6G) band using directional and quasi-omnidirectional antenna pairs. Measurements span 6.425-7.125 GHz at 32 matched positions per configuration in an open hall and an L-shaped corridor. System calibration and frequency-dependent peak-gain normalization retain antenna radiation-pattern weighting. Close-in and floating-intercept models are fitted to line-of-sight (LOS) and non-LOS (NLOS) path loss, respectively. Shadow-fading residuals, RMS delay spread (DS), and equivalent K factors derived from power delay profiles are characterized. LOS exponents range from 1.98 to 2.14. Despite similar attenuation slopes, directional links exhibit smaller LOS residuals and DS and higher equivalent K factors. Hall DS medians are 1.78 and 36.52 ns for directional and quasi-omnidirectional links. Corridor NLOS slopes are -1.12 and 2.54, respectively, while DS ordering varies by position. These results characterize antenna-dependent parameters for U6G indoor channels.
item.dc:creator: Chengsong Fu, Hongbo Zhao, Jianer Zhou, Xiongbin Yu, Weichao Li, Chen Zhuang, Meng Li, Wenquan Feng, Xiaofeng Tao

item.title: Medical Imaging Classification with Cold-Atom Reservoir Computing using Auto-Encoders and Surrogate-Driven Training
item.description: arXiv:2605.06727v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce a hybrid quantum-classical pipeline, based on neutral-atom reservoir computing, for medical image classification, focusing on the binary classification task of polyp detection. To deal effectively with the high dimensionality, we integrate a guided auto-encoder. This pipeline learns compact and discriminative representations of image data that are also well-suited for quantum reservoir computing. A key challenge in such systems is the non-differentiable nature of quantum measurements, which creates a 'gradient barrier' for standard training. We overcome this barrier by incorporating a differentiable surrogate model that emulates the quantum layer, enabling end-to-end backpropagation through the entire system. This guided training process is jointly optimized for classification accuracy and for faithful image recovery from the auto-encoder. The learned latent representations are encoded as pulse detuning parameters within a Rydberg Hamiltonian, and quantum embeddings are subsequently obtained through expectation values. These embeddings are then passed to a linear classifier. Our simulations show that this method outperforms some traditional approaches that use PCA or unguided autoencoders. We also conduct ablation studies to assess the impact of various quantum and training parameters, demonstrating the robustness and flexibility of our proposed pipeline for real-world medical imaging applications, even in the current NISQ era.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: 2025 IEEE International Conference on Quantum Artificial Intelligence (QAI)
